status_summary: EPA revisited the designation and kept it. The 2024 rule designating PFOA and PFOS as CERCLA hazardous substances took effect 2024-07-08; on 2025-09-17 EPA stated in a court filing in the Chamber of Commerce's challenge that it had finished its review and would keep the listing, said it would begin a rulemaking under CERCLA section 102(a) to set a framework for designating future hazardous substances, and said it would address liability for passive receivers within current authority while a full fix needs Congress. EPA's 2026-02-06 year-one release again lists the affirmation of the listing. On 2026-08-18 the D.C. Circuit denied all petitions in Chamber of Commerce v. EPA, No. 24-1193, leaving the designation in place. No proposed rule for the section 102(a) framework, no passive receiver rulemaking, no proposal to remove the designation and no revision of the groundwater cleanup rules for PFAS was found. Separately, on 2026-05-20 EPA proposed to extend the compliance deadline for the PFOA and PFOS drinking water limits from 2029-04-26 to 2031-04-26 for systems that request it.

timeline.event: EPA Administrator announces plans (month only given; first of month used) to work with Congress and industry on a liability framework that protects passive receivers that did not make or generate PFAS.

In a court filing in the Chamber of Commerce's challenge, EPA states it has finished its review and will keep the 2024 designation of PFOA and PFOS as CERCLA hazardous substances; it also announces a planned rulemaking under CERCLA section 102(a) for a framework to designate future hazardous substances and says a statutory fix on passive receiver liability needs Congress (law firm summaries).
EPA's year-one PFAS release lists the affirmation of the CERCLA hazardous substance listing for PFOA and PFOS among its actions; it names no other PFAS designations.

EPA proposes (91 FR, doc. 2026-10086) an exemption extending the PFOA and PFOS drinking water compliance deadline from 2029-04-26 to 2031-04-26 for systems that request it; this is under the Safe Drinking Water Act, not CERCLA.

The D.C. Circuit unanimously denies the petitions for review in Chamber of Commerce v. EPA, No. 24-1193, upholding the designation of PFOA and PFOS as CERCLA hazardous substances; law firm summaries note possible rehearing or Supreme Court review.

title: Revisit the CERCLA hazardous substance designation of PFAS chemicals
uncertainties: Stage is a judgment call. The Mandate says only to revisit the designation without stating an outcome; EPA did complete a review, but it kept and defended the listing, so the record is labeled diverged (0) rather than completed. EPA's own 2025-09-17 filing and press release were not reached; the September 2025 facts come from two law firm summaries, and the filing's court was not named in them (the later decision is in the D.C. Circuit). The D.C. Circuit decision date, docket number and holding come from Beveridge & Diamond and Alston & Bird summaries, not the opinion. The Alston page is dated by its URL month and the 2026-08-28 advisory label in search results. Federal Register queries for CERCLA and PFAS rules and proposals since 2025-01-20 found only the drinking water deadline proposal and a draft Contaminant Candidate List 6; no CERCLA designation framework proposal. The Unified Agenda entry for the section 102(a) rulemaking was not read. EPA's April 2025 passive receiver statement is dated by month only, from EPA's PFAS actions page. Not examined: the Mandate's groundwater cleanup recommendation beyond a Federal Register search, other PFAS designations proposed by the prior administration, and any rehearing petition.
